doc.title: Al Grey interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 3, 1995

title: With Benny Carter: learning to read and Pottstown schooling
summary: Grey replaces J.J. Johnson with Carter, who teaches him reading and ad-lib solos. He notes his Pottstown school music reading helped, and that Carter broke up his band for Hollywood.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Right place at the right time, and I took J.J. Johnson’s place in Benny Carter’s orchestra, see? And I went out with Benny Carter and this was 1945, see? And then after that, Benny Carter had such a great band where Benny Carter was a person that was tremendous help in teaching more how to read, and play ad lib solos see? Because back in those days most of our jazz musicians were great jazz artists, but many of them could not read.
So they had to do much of it by ear?

That’s the way it was. Just like Louis Armstrong, see? This is where Louis Armstrong — and from this finally, again coming from Pottstown, where there was only like five or six black families, I had that opportunity to go to the white school in Pottstown. And like I was like the only black kid in the junior high school band but we had Kenny Hines, another black kid, in the band in high school. And so this gave a privilege of learning how to read.
So you were able to read notes at that time.

Yes, see, so this has like been my history throughout life, this is how I was able to get in the band from reading. And so this is when Benny Carter accepted me, but then Benny Carter, after a year after that, he broke up his band to go into the studios out in Hollywood, to write for movies and he became very famous with “Peyton Place,” and see, which back in those times no one ever knew it because they didn’t give you credit for that at that time, see?
